For Delhi’s outdoor workers, every heatwave has a price
On the frontlines of the climate crisis, street vendors and other outdoor workers in the Indian capital find both their health and their livelihoods at risk

Kamlesh Devi spends up to 12 hours each day at her roadside stall in Delhi, where rising temperatures are taking a toll on her health and livelihood. Credit: Safina Nabi
At a glance
This summer, parts of Delhi have recorded ‘feels-like’ temperatures of over 51°C. For the millions of the city’s residents who work outdoors, those temperatures are a serious threat.
For many, financial need all but forbids staying home – and in any case, home often offers little respite from the heat.
Researchers point out that extreme heat is a health-risk multiplier, hitting the vulnerable the hardest. Poverty, already associated with poorer health outcomes, deepens in temperatures that arrest trade, and a bout of heat-related sickness can spell financial disaster.
“The heat hits me directly. There is no shade, no fan, not even water,” says 60-year-old Kamlesh Devi, who spends 12 hours a day at her makeshift roadside stall in Delhi. “Sometimes I fall sick and can’t work. Then there is no income, and whatever little emergency savings I have end up going towards doctors and medical tests.”
Every morning by09:00, Kamlesh travels from Gurugram to Malviya Nagar, where she sells piggy banks, gift items, kitchenware and decorative pieces in the open. A mother of four married daughters, she has made that journey for years. But as Delhi’s summers become hotter and more humid, the work that once sustained her has become increasingly difficult.
This summer, the heat pushed her body beyond its limits. She fainted three times while at work. “The shopkeepers nearby picked me up,” she recalls. At a nearby government hospital, doctors said she was dehydrated and that her blood pressure had spiked dangerously on two occasions.
Kamlesh’s experience is far from unique, unfolding against the backdrop of one of Delhi’s hottest summers. In April, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued heatwave warnings across all districts of the capital, forecasting temperatures of 42–44°C – around 6°C above normal for the time of year. In May, Safdarjung, in the city’s south, recorded a maximum temperature of 43.6°C and the city’s warmest night in 14 years. In late June, high humidity pushed the ‘feels-like’ temperature to 51.3°C, making prolonged outdoor work even more hazardous.
Yet staying home is fraught. On a good day, Kamlesh makes sales worth 500 to 1,000 rupees (about US$ 6–12), earning a profit of around 300 to 350 rupees (US$ 3.50–4). At this income level, it’s hard to save up a financial cushion to provide for days off. And lately, her earnings have begun to slip. “There are days when the heat and humidity are so terrible that no one comes to my stall. Even after sitting here all day, I go home empty-handed,” she says. “Sometimes I pack up because I start feeling nauseous. Other days, I don’t come at all.”
A health-risk multiplier
For thousands of people who earn a living outdoors, extreme heat is no longer merely making work more uncomfortable, it is reshaping their health, livelihoods and daily routines. Workers describe skipping meals because they lose their appetite, cutting their working hours, watching customers disappear during the hottest parts of the day and returning home exhausted, only to find little relief from the heat.
In a 2026 study, the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED) described extreme heat as a “risk multiplier”, amplifying existing inequalities rather than affecting everyone equally. For informal workers, the consequences extend beyond the workplace. Low incomes, insecure housing, limited savings and poor access to healthcare combine to create a cycle in which illness reduces earnings, medical expenses deplete household resources, and recovery becomes increasingly difficult.
Kamlesh’s experience reflects a broader national trend. The 2025 Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change found that Indians experienced an average of 19.8 heatwave days in 2024, with 6.6 of those days attributable to climate change. The report also estimated that heat exposure resulted in the loss of 247 billion potential labour hours in 2024; a record high, equivalent to about 419 hours per person and 124% higher than the 1990–1999 average.
The burden fell disproportionately on people whose livelihoods depend on working outdoors. Agriculture accounted for 66% of the labour-hour losses, while construction made up another 20%, highlighting the growing toll of extreme heat on outdoor workers. The associated loss in potential income was estimated at US$ 194 billion.
In response, Delhi’s Heat Action Plan includes public advisories, early warnings and measures to reduce heat exposure. Yet for many informal workers, earning a daily wage still means remaining outdoors despite dangerous temperatures, with limited access to shade, drinking water or cooling facilities.
Unendurable summers
Kamlesh’s struggle is echoed on pavements and street corners across the city, where workers exposed to the elements describe a summer that is becoming increasingly difficult to endure.
Among them is Abrar Ahmad, a fruit vendor.
“We dry up in the sun all day, and by evening I have to figure out whether I have made a profit or a loss,” says Abrar Ahmad, a fruit vendor who has lived in South Delhi for nearly 30 years after migrating from Badaun in Uttar Pradesh.
Each morning, Abrar pushes his handcart through the streets, selling seasonal fruits under the open sky. He says the heat is taking a growing toll, not only on his health but also on the fruit he depends on for his livelihood.
“The heat is gruesome. Sometimes the fruits spoil before I can sell them, and that means a loss,” he says.
At home, there is little respite. Abrar lives with his wife and two daughters, a four-year-old and a three-month-old, in a single rented room with a small attached kitchen and bathroom.
“When I fall sick, I can’t work. But when my wife or children get sick, my work suffers then too,” he says. “We all live in one small room without ventilation. This is what we can afford.”
Medicine meets meteorology
Public health physician and policy expert Dr Chandrakant Lahariya says stories like Kamlesh’s and Abrar’s demonstrate why extreme heat should no longer be viewed solely as a weather event.
“Heat affects people in multiple ways. The most immediate impact is dehydration, which can lead to heatstroke if left untreated. Extreme heat also has broader social consequences, reducing energy levels and productivity, particularly among outdoor workers. Many of them also lack access to safe drinking water, increasing the risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance,” he says.
“From a public health perspective, protecting outdoor workers from heat is now an urgent priority. Governments should establish cooling points with access to clean drinking water and oral rehydration solutions, and create shaded rest shelters where workers can recover from heat exposure, much like the winter shelters set up during the colder months,” Lahariya added.
As climate change drives hotter and longer summers, protecting those who spend their working lives outdoors may become one of India’s defining public health and labour challenges. For millions who cannot afford to stay indoors, the cost of a hotter city is both financial and physical. It risks becoming existential.

Record heatwave grips Asia as potatoes ‘boil’ in fields, lions perish The crop, grown in South Korea’s Gangwon province, had appeared healthy just a week earlier. But when Lee dug into the soil, he found the potatoes were ‘like boiled potatoes’. Potatoes are ‘boiling’ in the ground, lions are dying at a zoo, as record heat is gripping swathes of Asia, with extreme temperatures affecting South Korea, Hong Kong, Japan and China. Most of South Korea has been reeling under an intense heatwave, with temperatures in the densely populated greater Seoul area, home to 20 million people, and adjacent areas soaring to nearly 40°C (104°F), local media reported. ‘Boiled potatoes’ In Yanghu, around 130km north-east of Seoul, farmer Lee Sang-hyuk discovered that many of his potatoes had been destroyed by the extreme heat. The crop, grown in South Korea’s Gangwon province, had appeared healthy just a week earlier. But when Lee dug into the soil, he found the potatoes were ‘like boiled potatoes’. “It’s not just one or two fields like this. How can I even put it into words? It’s so upsetting,” he was quoted as saying by The Guardian. Lee’s damaged harvest is among the latest examples of the impact of an intense summer across East Asia, with South Korea, Japan and Hong Kong experiencing extreme temperatures in recent weeks. On August 2, the south-eastern city of Yangsan recorded 42.5°C, the highest temperature ever recorded in South Korea since modern weather records began in 1904. Meanwhile, Japan’s anti-disaster agency reported that more than 18,000 people with heatstroke symptoms were transported to hospitals during the week of July 20 to 26. Three lions have died at a Tokyo zoo, while a number of other animals have developed apparent heatstroke symptoms, news agency AP reported. The extreme heat hit despite an El Niño event being underway. The natural climate pattern has previously been linked to a lower likelihood of extreme summer heat in Japan. In Hong Kong, the observatory recorded 36.9°C, the highest temperature there since records began in 1884. The city was experiencing the effects of Typhoon Dolphin, whose outer bands pushed hot air across the region. ‘Red warning is clearly set too high’ The record heat also highlighted shortcomings in Hong Kong’s heat stress warning system for outdoor workers, which remained at its lowest level even as temperatures hit a record high. “The threshold for the red warning is clearly set too high”, Lam Chiu Ying, a former head of the Hong Kong Observatory, wrote on Facebook, according to The Guardian. “If even a record-breaking temperature can’t trigger it, isn’t it just a display piece used to decorate a shop window?” Following the criticism, Hong Kong’s Labour Department said it was reviewing the warning system in consultation with the observatory. China has also faced intense heat. A weather station in the western Xinjiang region recorded 50°C in July, while heatwaves affected parts of the north-east. In North Korea, Pyongyang experienced a series of tropical nights, with temperatures remaining above 25°C even overnight. Heatstroke can be dangerous and come on more quickly than you realise. With temperatures rocketing in parts of England and Wales, it’s important to know how to recognise the signs.
Spending too much time in the heat or overly exerting yourself in the sun can cause heatstroke.
During the heatwaves we’ve increasingly experienced in recent years, health officials have reiterated how important it is to prevent children and older people from falling victim to the high temperatures. But would you know how to tell heat exhaustion from heatstroke?
Symptoms of heat exhaustion
Heat exhaustion is what happens when the body overheats and cannot cool down. It usually doesn’t require emergency medical attention, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), as long as you can cool yourself down within 30 minutes.

If you do not take action to cool down, heat exhaustion can lead to heatstroke, which is a lot more serious.
Symptoms of heatstroke
Heatstroke is where the body is no longer able to cool down and your body’s temperature becomes dangerously high.

Heatstroke is a medical emergency. If you think someone has heatstroke you should dial 999 and then try to cool them down.
How to treat heat exhaustion
Dr Luke Powles, from Bupa Health Clinics, previously told HuffPost UK people exhibiting symptoms of heat exhaustion should be cooled down as a priority.
“Move them into a cool place, get them to lie down and put their feet up,” he explained. “Give them plenty of water and cool their skin with a cold pack, or towel.”
It might also help to remove unnecessary items of clothing, like socks. You could also fan them to try and cool them down.
The person should start feeling better within 30 minutes – if not, it is very important to seek medical help immediately.
How to prevent heat exhaustion and heatstroke
Stay hydrated by drinking plenty of cool drinks and avoid alcohol. It’s also beneficial to keep cool by: wearing light fabrics, avoiding the sun between 11am and 3pm, sprinkling water over your skin and taking cool showers.
Avoid exercising and try to keep your home cool by closing curtains and windows, and turning off electrical equipment or lights.
When to get urgent help
If heatstroke symptoms progress to the ones listed below – or the person is no better after 30 minutes – you should call 999.
They feel hot and dry.
They aren’t sweating even though they are too hot. Their skin might also look red – this can be harder to spot on brown and Black skin, according to the NHS.
They have a very high temperature that’s risen to 40°C or above.
They have rapid breathing or shortness of breath.
They’re confused.
They have a fit (seizure).
They lose consciousness (if this happens, put them in the recovery position while you wait for help).
They are unresponsive.

UK weather outlook: Could today be the hottest day of the year as the heatwave peaks today?
The latest heatwave peaks today, with temperatures climbing into the high 30s across much of England. Could the UK see its hottest day of the year today, and could we set a new August record?
After several days of steadily rising temperatures, Thursday marks the peak of this latest spell of hot weather.
High pressure remains firmly in control across much of England and Wales, bringing widespread sunshine and drawing very warm air north from the continent.
Temperatures are forecast to reach the mid-30s across a large part of England and Wales, with highs of 37°C or even 38°C possible in one or two locations across central and western England.
Should temperatures exceed 38°C, it would become the hottest day of the year so far.
The current UK August record stands at 38.5°C, although breaking that record remains relatively unlikely.
A Met Office amber extreme heat warning remains in force across parts of central and eastern England until the end of today.
Thunderstorms in the north and west
While southern areas enjoy the sunshine, the weather will be far more unsettled across the north and west.
A weather front moving into Scotland and Northern Ireland will trigger heavy showers and thunderstorms during Thursday.
Northern Ireland faces the greatest risk of downpours, frequent lightning, gusty winds and large hail, where a Met Office yellow warning is in force.
Further heavy rain will affect northern and western Scotland, while isolated thunderstorms are also possible across southern and eastern Scotland and into northwest England.
Fresher air arrives on Friday
The intense heat begins to ease from the west overnight as a weakening weather front introduces fresher Atlantic air.
By Friday, Scotland, Northern Ireland, Wales and western England will all feel noticeably cooler, with temperatures generally reaching the high teens or low 20s in the north and west.
The southeast will hold onto the hottest conditions for another day, with highs still reaching the low or even mid-30s in places, although temperatures will be several degrees lower than Thursday's peak.
Elsewhere across England, highs will mostly be in the mid to high 20s, with a few showers developing, particularly across Wales and southern England.
Cooler weekend, but rain remains uncertain
The bigger change arrives during the weekend as temperatures fall back closer to seasonal average across the UK.
Saturday may bring a few showers, particularly from the northwest and perhaps into south eastern areas, although confidence remains lower than earlier in the week.
Despite earlier indications of rain, Sunday is now expected to be largely dry for many places, with sunny spells and much more comfortable temperatures replacing the recent heat.
Will next week finally bring rain?
Weather models continue to suggest a spell of rain could move southeast across the UK late on Monday or Tuesday, although there remains uncertainty over both the timing and intensity.
Some heavier bursts are possible along the frontal system, but even if the rain arrives, it is expected to move through relatively quickly.
This is unlikely to deliver the prolonged rainfall needed to significantly ease drought conditions across many parts of England, with much of the rain likely to run off the very dry ground rather than being absorbed.
Beyond that, models continue to disagree over whether low pressure will become more dominant or whether high pressure quickly re-establishes itself, making confidence through the latter part of next week much lower.

New Delhi/Ghaziabad: Amid fresh forecasts of heavy rain and thunderstorm, authorities in the Ghaziabad and Fariadabad areas of Delhi NCR have issued a yellow alert from Thursday, warning people to exercise caution amid forecasts of heavy rain and lightning. The advisory comes following recent deadly incidents during storms in the region.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast predicts heavy rain and lightning starting today and continuing through Sunday (August 17). Rain and thundershowers are forecast in Gurugram as well.
On July 9, at least three people, including two children, lost their lives in heavy rain-related incidents in Ghaziabad. One of them was killed after being trapped under the debris of a house wall, which collapsed in the Loni area.
A 5-year-old boy, Mohammad Saad, and a 3-year-old child died after drowning in accumulated rainwater, while 50-year-old Ram Ajit Rai lost his life after being crushed by a collapsing wall. The administration has provided financial assistance of Rs 4 lakh each to the next of kin of the victims.
People push a school bus stuck at a waterlogged road due to heavy rain at Vasundhara, in Ghaziabad on Jul 09, 2026 (File/ANI Video Grab) Following this, the administration has instructed all departments to remain on high alert. People were advised to stay away from old, dilapidated buildings and kachcha (unreinforced/mud) walls.
Instructions have also been issued to securely fasten tin sheds and other materials used in construction sites during strong winds and rain and for people to maintain a safe distance from construction areas.
Additional District Magistrate (Finance and Revenue) Ajni Kumar Singh said that the fresh advisories have been issued based on the IMD forecast. “A Yellow Alert has been mandated due to the likelihood of heavy rain and lightning between August 13 and August 16,” he said, citing the IMD forecast.
The administration has appealed to the public to avoid stepping out unnecessarily during inclement weather and to stay updated on weather reports to prevent any untoward incidents. They also urged people to avoid unnecessary travel during bad weather and to stay indoors unless absolutely essential. “Seeking shelter under trees during strong winds and rain can be dangerous and even fatal,” officials said.
A special advisory has also been issued for farmers, urging them not to visit their fields during heavy rain and storms to ensure safety and prevent loss of life.
The district administration has urged the public to stay updated with official weather-related information via social media and other channels.
“Residents are advised to use the India Meteorological Department's official mobile application for accurate weather updates. Caution is the best course of action during the ‘Yellow Alert’ period over the next four days. Adhering to guidelines can significantly minimise the risk of loss of life and property during potential heavy rains and strong storms,” they said.
Meanwhile, the weather department said that temperatures are set to drop over the next week, hovering at about 33 degrees Celsius by Wednesday for Noida and Ghaziabad and 34 degrees Celsius for Gurugram. Faridabad will record 31 degrees.
The IMD further said that winds will stay gentle, and sunrise/sunset times are pretty steady.

When is the best time to go outside?
Plan frequent rest breaks in shaded or air-conditioned areas, especially during strenuous work or physical activity.
Are you wearing the right clothing and sunscreen?
When going outside in hot weather:
- Wear loose-fitting, lightweight clothing that allows your body to cool properly.
- Wear a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses.
Are you staying hydrated?
Drinking plenty of fluids helps your body sweat and maintain its temperature.

Guwahati (Assam) [India], August 13 : The Assam Christian Forum on Thursday welcomed the government's decision to refer the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) for detailed examination, saying the move would enable wider consultation and dialogue.
The Forum also expressed gratitude to the government and said the decision demonstrated its willingness to listen to the concerns of NGOs, minority communities and other civil society stakeholders.
Assam Christian Forum spokeperson, Allen Brooks, stated that "We also offer heartfelt thanks to God for His gracious intervention in guiding this process towards greater consultation and dialogue. This democratic and consultative step demonstrates the Government's willingness to listen to the concerns of the NGOs, Minority communities and other civil society stakeholders."
Brooks said the Forum looks forward to constructive engagement with the Ministry of Home Affairs and the JPC during the scrutiny of the proposed legislation.
He said the Forum, which works in areas including education, healthcare, social development and charitable initiatives, remains committed to contributing to the country's progress.
"We reaffirm our readiness to work in a spirit of dialogue and cooperation to help shape a balanced statutory frameworkone that upholds natural justice while enabling genuine civil society organisations to continue their service to the nation and its citizens without hindrance," Brooks said.
He further said the Forum remains committed to transparency, accountability and responsible engagement with the government and other stakeholders.
"We pray that the deliberations of the Joint Parliamentary Committee will be guided by wisdom, fairness and the common good," Brooks said.
